newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- No Fed move seen at July 1-2 FOMC.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- No Fed move seen at July 1-2 FOMC.

text.p: A recent string of soft economic data coupled with some political pressures will deter Federal Reserve monetary policymakers from raising short-term interest rates at their July 1-2 meeting, economists said in a Reuters poll.
All but one of 36 analysts polled on Tuesday and Wednesday said the central bank would leave the federal funds rate unchanged at 5.50 percent. One expert said he was undecided.
Fourteen of 36 pundits said the Fed would also hold rates steady at the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on August 19.
Fourteen experts said monetary policymakers would vote to boost rates by 25 basis points in August, and the rest said they were uncertain.
Forecasts in the latest poll differed dramatically from the Reuters poll conducted on June 2, when 20 of 37 economists projected a Fed rate hike in July.
The economists said that with jobs in abundance and low inflation, there would not be any justification for an interest-rate hike at this time.
For most Americans, low unemployment is good news, noted Kurt Karl, chief economist at WEFA Inc's U.S. forecasting center.
"The Fed seems to have backed off on rates in the face of growth and unemployment," said Karl, explaining that the Fed is mostly concerned with signs of future inflation.
But recent economic data suggested inflation remains tame.

The U.S. Labor Department reported the Consumer Price Index inched 0.1 percent in May versus a 0.1-percent rise in the previous month. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, CPI rose 0.2 percent, lower than the 0.3-percent rise in April.
"If CPI had been 0.4 percent, we would have had a good chance of the Fed raising interest rates," added Karl.

Despite the fact that a high percentage of Americans are now part of the workforce, which is evidenced by the 4.8-percent jobless rate in May, consumers have become more frugal with their spending habits, economists said.
Christopher Probyn, senior economist at UBS Securities Inc, said that the first-quarter strength in consumer demand had waned, noting the slowdown in retail sales data in May.
"Since June, we have had not only a weak retail sales report for May, but we have had downward revisions to March and April," Probyn said.
Retail sales fell 0.1 percent in May and 0.9 percent in April, and were revised down to unchanged in March.

He said that the Fed had justified its reason for lifting interest rates in March because there was evidence of persistent strength in demand. "Clearly, there is no strength in demand (at this time)," he added.
In addition to a softening of the U.S. economy, a few experts said that political forces may also weigh on the Fed's decision to keep rates on hold.
"Right now, I think the Fed is concerned about the political jawboning that has gone on in the last few months," said David Blitzer, chief economist at Standard & Poor's.
"The politics say if you can't see inflation, you're going to get skewered for fighting it, and the politics are going to delay the move until August," he said.
Paul Kasriel, chief economist at Northern Trust Co in Chicago, agreed. The central bank is in a very difficult political environment to be preemptive, he said.

"The Fed really needs more of a smoking gun before it can act," Kasriel said, adding that the Fed was probably surprised and concerned about the criticism it had received from both political parties following the March 25 tightening.
"So it is a bipartisan criticism of the Fed now," he said. "With inflation still low, there is no constituency out there to fight inflation."
